title: Ecclesiastes 3:9–22
context: Ecclesiastes 3:9–22 reflects on the poem of times. The Preacher asks what profit a worker has, sees the burden God has given, and confesses that “He has made everything beautiful in its time” and has set eternity in human hearts, yet people cannot find out God’s work from beginning to end (3:11; compare 8:17). He commends joy, doing good, eating, drinking, and enjoying one’s labor as “the gift of God” (3:13; compare 2:24; 5:18–19), and says that whatever God does is forever, so that people fear before him (3:14). Seeing wickedness in the place of justice, he trusts that God will judge the righteous and the wicked (3:16–17; compare 11:9; 12:14). He then observes that humans, like animals, die, have one breath, and return to dust (3:18–20; compare Genesis 3:19; Psalm 49:12, 20), and asks who knows whether the human spirit goes upward (3:21), a question that stands alongside 12:7, where the spirit returns to God who gave it. Readers take 3:18–21 in different ways: as the honest limit of what can be seen under the sun, as a challenge to human pride, or as a question to be read beside 12:7 without being harmonized with it. These readings are found in both traditions. The meaning of “God seeks again that which is passed away” (3:15) is also discussed. Both traditions treat 3:11 and 3:14 as largely shared ground about God’s sovereign ordering and human limits; questions about how divine direction relates to human freedom are treated in the existing boxes at Proverbs 16:9 and Proverbs 21:1.

verses.text: What profit has he who works in that in which he labors?
verses.arminianNotes:
The Preacher asks, “What profit has he who works in that in which he labors?” The question echoes 1:3.

Arminian readers note that the question challenges any attempt to find ultimate meaning in labor alone, and they see it as an invitation to look beyond work for what truly lasts, while still valuing honest work as part of life.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the question arises from the poem of times: if every action has its season, human toil cannot secure lasting gain by itself, and they see the Preacher preparing to point toward God’s work and gifts.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the limits of human labor seen under the sun.

verses.text: I have seen the burden which God has given to the sons of men to be afflicted with.
verses.arminianNotes:
He says he has seen the burden God has given to the sons of men to be afflicted with. The word burden may also be taken as a task or occupation.

Arminian readers note the honest acknowledgment that life brings hard tasks, and they see the Preacher naming the weight of human toil without despair, as a starting point for wisdom and trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the burden is described as given by God, which places even the hardships of human labor within his purposes, and they see the verse as setting up the confession in 3:11 that God has made everything beautiful in its time.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the weight and the limits of human toil.

verses.text: He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.
verses.arminianNotes:
He says, “He has made everything beautiful in its time” and that God has set eternity in human hearts, yet people cannot find out the work God has done from beginning to end. The verse joins wonder and limit.

Arminian readers note that the longing for eternity is a gift that draws people to seek God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that God makes everything beautiful in its time, and they see the limit on human understanding as a call to trust. The meaning of the word rendered eternity is discussed.

Both traditions treat the verse as largely shared ground about God’s ordering and human limits, and they leave the questions treated at Proverbs 16:9 and 21:1 to those boxes rather than reopening them here.

verses.text: I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice, and to do good as long as they live.
verses.arminianNotes:
He knows that there is nothing better for people than to rejoice and to do good as long as they live. Joy and goodness are commended.

Arminian readers note that the Preacher’s counsel joins enjoyment with doing good, and they see a call to live gratefully and generously within the limits of a life whose larger pattern cannot be fully understood.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that this is one of several passages in which the Preacher commends joy (compare 2:24; 8:15; 9:7), and they see it as a sober and positive counsel to receive life with thanksgiving rather than with restless striving.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about joy and goodness as fitting responses to God’s gifts.

verses.text: Also that every man should eat and drink, and enjoy good in all his labor, is the gift of God.
verses.arminianNotes:
He adds that every person’s eating, drinking, and enjoying good in all his labor is “the gift of God.” The ordinary pleasures of life are received from God.

Arminian readers note that the gift is meant to be received and enjoyed, and they see the verse as encouraging people to accept God’s good gifts with gratitude rather than to despise them in the name of seriousness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that enjoyment itself is God’s gift (compare 2:24, where it is “from the hand of God”), and they see the verse as a reminder that even the capacity to enjoy one’s labor depends on his grace.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about receiving everyday blessings as gifts from God.

verses.text: I know that whatever God does, it shall be forever. Nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it; and God has done it, that men should fear before him.
verses.arminianNotes:
He knows that whatever God does shall be forever, that nothing can be added to it or taken from it, and that God has done it so that people should fear before him.

Arminian readers note that God’s works are lasting and reliable, and they see the fear of God as a reverent response that people are called to give freely.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the permanence and completeness of God’s work, and they see the fear of God as the fitting response to his sovereign rule (compare 12:13).

Both traditions treat the verse as largely shared ground about God’s enduring work and the fear of him. The question of how divine direction relates to human choice is treated at Proverbs 16:9 and 21:1.

verses.text: That which is has been long ago, and that which is to be has been long ago. God seeks again that which is passed away.
verses.arminianNotes:
He says that what is has been long ago, and what is to be has been long ago, and that God seeks again that which is passed away. The last clause is difficult and is read in several ways.

Arminian readers note the echo of 1:9, “there is no new thing under the sun”, and they see the verse as humbling human claims to novelty and control.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the final clause may mean that God brings back what has passed, that he calls the past to account, or that he seeks what has been driven away, and they hold the meaning open.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the recurring patterns of history under God’s rule, and neither builds doctrine on the uncertain final clause.

verses.text: Moreover I saw under the sun, in the place of justice, that wickedness was there; and in the place of righteousness, that wickedness was there.
verses.arminianNotes:
He sees under the sun that wickedness is found in the place of justice and in the place of righteousness. Injustice reaches even the courts.

Arminian readers note that the Preacher refuses to hide the reality of corrupted justice, and they see in this honesty a call for people to oppose injustice and to seek righteousness in their own dealings.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the observation of corrupted justice leads directly to confidence in God’s judgment in the next verse, and they see the Preacher’s realism about human institutions as consistent with Scripture’s teaching about the effects of sin.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the grievous reality of injustice and the longing for righteous judgment.

verses.text: I said in my heart, “God will judge the righteous and the wicked; for there is a time there for every purpose and for every work.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He says in his heart, “God will judge the righteous and the wicked; for there is a time there for every purpose and for every work.” The poem of times now includes a time of judgment.

Arminian readers note that the coming judgment confirms that human choices matter and that people are accountable for them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the word there may point to God’s appointed time of judgment, whether in this life or beyond it, and they see the verse as anticipating the book’s close (compare 12:14, “For God will bring every work into judgment”).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: God will judge rightly, even when human courts fail.

verses.text: I said in my heart, “As for the sons of men, God tests them, so that they may see that they themselves are like animals.
verses.arminianNotes:
He says in his heart that God tests the sons of men so that they may see that they themselves are like animals. The verse begins a hard reflection on mortality.

Arminian readers note that the testing reveals human frailty and is meant to humble people, and they see the comparison with animals as a warning against pride rather than a denial of human dignity.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the verse as exposing human pride, and they note that the comparison concerns what is visible under the sun, especially death, which falls on people as on animals.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and hold together the Preacher’s sober realism with the rest of Scripture’s teaching that humans are made in God’s image.

verses.text: For that which happens to the sons of men happens to animals. Even one thing happens to them. As the one dies, so the other dies. Yes, they have all one breath; and man has no advantage over the animals, for all is vanity.
verses.arminianNotes:
What happens to people happens to animals: one dies as the other dies, they all have one breath, and man has no advantage over the animals, for all is vanity. The breath recalls the breath of life in Genesis 2:7.

Arminian readers note the honest realism about death, which comes to all creatures alike.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the parallel with Psalm 49:12, “He is like the animals that perish”, and they see the verse as describing what can be observed of death under the sun rather than giving a full account of human destiny.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about mortality and hold its strong language within the book’s wider perspective.

verses.text: All go to one place. All are from the dust, and all turn to dust again.
verses.arminianNotes:
All go to one place; all are from the dust, and all turn to dust again. The words echo Genesis 3:19, “For you are dust, and you shall return to dust.”

Arminian readers note that the verse reminds every reader of the shared mortal condition, and they see it as a call to humility and to living wisely in the time that is given.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the one place is most naturally the grave, and they see the verse as consistent with Psalm 104:29, “You take away their breath; they die and return to the dust”, a sober picture of mortality under God’s hand.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and do not take it as the Bible’s final word on life after death.

verses.text: Who knows the spirit of man, whether it goes upward, and the spirit of the animal, whether it goes downward to the earth?”
verses.arminianNotes:
He asks, “Who knows the spirit of man, whether it goes upward, and the spirit of the animal, whether it goes downward to the earth?” The WEB renders the verse as a question; some translations take it as a description of the spirit that goes upward.

Arminian readers often read the question as the limit of what can be known under the sun, and they set it beside 12:7, where “the spirit returns to God who gave it”, without harmonizing the two.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers often read it similarly, while some in both traditions see the question as genuinely open within the book.

Both traditions present these readings side by side, hedge them, and treat the verse as shared ground rather than a point of division.

verses.text: Therefore I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his works, for that is his portion; for who can bring him to see what will be after him?
verses.arminianNotes:
He sees that there is nothing better than for a person to rejoice in his works, for that is his portion, since no one can show him what will come after him. The reflection ends in counsel.

Arminian readers note that the inability to know the future frees people to receive the present as a gift and to work joyfully rather than anxiously.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the portion is a word the book uses for what God gives (compare 5:18; 9:9), and they see the counsel as an invitation to contentment under God’s hand while the future remains in his keeping.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about joy in one’s work and humble acceptance that the future is unknown to human beings.
